name: Collecting duct carcinoma
aliases: carcinoma of the collecting ducts of Bellini

clinicalPearls: A rare, aggressive renal carcinoma arising from the collecting ducts of Bellini in the renal medulla
Tends to present at a younger age than clear cell carcinoma, often with advanced disease
Common presenting features include haematuria, flank pain, an abdominal mass and constitutional symptoms
Imaging typically shows a centrally located, infiltrative medullary mass rather than a well-defined cortical tumour
Histology shows irregular tubular and papillary structures with a marked desmoplastic stromal reaction
It behaves more like an aggressive urothelial cancer than a typical renal cell carcinoma
Early lymph node and distant metastases are frequent at diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: Collecting duct carcinoma originates from the principal cells of the distal collecting ducts within the medulla. It is a high-grade tumour with infiltrative growth, extensive desmoplasia and early vascular and lymphatic invasion. Its central medullary origin explains the infiltrative imaging pattern and the tendency to involve the renal pelvis and regional nodes. Its biology overlaps with high-grade urothelial carcinoma, and it is distinguished from renal medullary carcinoma by retained SMARCB1 expression and the absence of an obligatory link to sickling haemoglobinopathies.
additionalDifferentials: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma with infiltrative growth
Renal pelvis inflammatory or infective mass
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis to define the infiltrative mass and nodal spread
Tissue diagnosis with immunohistochemistry to distinguish from urothelial and medullary carcinoma
Urine cytology and evaluation of the upper urinary tract
Baseline renal function and staging investigations
redFlags: Infiltrative central renal mass with haematuria and systemic symptoms
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally poor, with many patients presenting at an advanced stage and limited response to systemic therapy; complete surgical resection of localised disease offers the best chance of prolonged survival.
pitfalls: Mistaking an infiltrative medullary tumour for upper tract urothelial carcinoma or vice versa
Attributing a central renal mass to infection and delaying oncological work-up
Assuming standard clear cell targeted therapy will be effective
Underestimating the likelihood of occult metastatic disease
references: WHO Classification of Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
management: Radical nephrectomy with regional lymph node dissection is the standard curative approach for localised, resectable disease
Complete surgical resection of localised disease is the single most important determinant of prolonged survival
Thorough preoperative staging with cross sectional abdominal and pelvic imaging plus chest imaging is important before surgery given the tendency for early nodal and distant spread

No established histology specific role for routine adjuvant systemic therapy exists in CDC, adjuvant kinase inhibitor and other adjuvant approaches in renal cell carcinoma broadly have shown inconsistent or no survival benefit, so this remains case by case with trial consideration
Advanced or metastatic CDC is generally treated with urothelial type cytotoxic chemotherapy principles rather than the clear cell renal cell carcinoma targeted therapy or immunotherapy paradigm
Platinum based cytotoxic combination chemotherapy is the systemic treatment most commonly used for advanced or metastatic CDC

Standard clear cell renal cell carcinoma agents such as VEGF pathway tyrosine kinase inhibitors, mTOR inhibitors, and checkpoint inhibitor combinations generally show poor response in CDC given its distinct biology
Clinical trial enrolment should be considered whenever available given the limited evidence base and poor response to conventional systemic agents
Best supportive and palliative care with symptom control should run alongside active treatment discussions from diagnosis of advanced disease
Structured surveillance imaging after resection of localised disease is warranted to detect recurrence early given the aggressive natural history
Baseline and interval renal function assessment should accompany oncological staging and follow up
New haematuria, flank pain, palpable mass, or constitutional symptoms after treatment should prompt prompt re-imaging
All suspected or confirmed CDC should be managed through a specialist uro-oncology multidisciplinary team from diagnosis
Refer for genitourinary pathology review with immunohistochemistry when diagnosis is uncertain to exclude upper tract urothelial carcinoma and renal medullary carcinoma
